0.title: Last Words: The Final Letter of the Apostle Paul
0.overview:
There is a letter that reads like a last will and testament, a soldier’s final dispatch from the front, and a father’s farewell to his son — all at once. Paul writes 2 Timothy from a Roman dungeon, probably the Mamertine Prison below the Capitoline Hill, where prisoners awaited execution. He has already stood before Nero’s tribunal; he expects to stand there again, and this time he does not expect to survive. He has been abandoned by most of his colleagues. Demas has gone back to the world. The churches of Asia have turned away. The winter is coming and he has no cloak. Only Luke is with him.

And yet the letter is not a cry of despair but an act of faith. Paul is not finished. He is fighting, praying, thinking, teaching to the last. He writes to Timothy — the son of his heart, the young man he circumcised and took on mission, who is now in Ephesus struggling with false teachers and the creeping temptation to soft-pedal the gospel for the sake of peace — and he writes with the urgency of a man who knows the window is closing. Guard the deposit. Don’t be ashamed. Endure suffering. Preach the word. These are not polite suggestions; they are dying instructions.

The letter is the most personal in the Pauline corpus. More than anywhere else we see Paul the man: Paul who longs for Timothy’s tears, who is comforted by Onesiphorus’s courage, who feels the sting of Alexander’s opposition, who in his final lines sends greetings from people whose names he has not forgotten. The great apostle is a human being who is cold, lonely, and facing death — and whose faith in the Jesus who appears in this letter (“remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead”) is, in the end, the only thing that has not shaken.

The letter is addressed to the minister, but it speaks to every Christian who must hold something precious in a world that does not want it. The deposit Paul entrusts to Timothy — the gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen — is the same deposit entrusted to every generation of the church. Guard it. Pass it on. It is worth dying for. Paul’s life proves the claim.

1.title: Guard the Deposit: Courage, the Gospel, and Faithful Examples
1.overview:
Chapter 1 opens with Paul’s most affectionate letter opening: he thinks of Timothy constantly, longs to see him, remembers his tears, and is confident of his genuine faith — a faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. The warmth is not merely emotional; it is the foundation from which Paul presses his most urgent charge: stir up the gift of God in you, for God has not given us a spirit of fear but of power and love and self-control.

The theological engine of the chapter is the great gospel passage of vv. 8–12, where Paul — who is about to urge Timothy to suffer for the gospel — articulates what that gospel is: God’s sovereign purpose formed before time began, brought to light in the appearing of Jesus Christ who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. The foundation of courage is not personal confidence but the character of the One whose gospel we carry.

The chapter ends with two contrasting examples: the entire province of Asia, which has turned away from Paul, and Onesiphorus, who searched for the imprisoned apostle in Rome and was not ashamed of his chains. Timothy is being invited to choose between these two responses to the gospel and its herald.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul writes as an apostle by God's will, “according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus” (v.1) — to Timothy, his beloved child: grace, mercy and peace (v.2).

Both details matter. Paul is in Rome, in prison, and this time does not expect to come out; chapter 4 will say the time of his departure has come. These are the last written words we have from him — and he opens by naming his commission in terms of life. And where the first letter called Timothy “my true child in the faith”, set against the counterfeits then circulating, here he is “my beloved child.” The polemical edge is gone.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Personal Letter, Not a Church Order

There is no thanksgiving for a congregation here because no congregation is in view. 1 Timothy was a manual for a man running a difficult church; this is an old man writing to a younger one while there is still time. The difference shapes everything that follows — the tears remembered in verse 4, the grandmother named in verse 5, the request in chapter 4 to bring a cloak and some parchments.

'Mercy' appears in the greeting again, as in the first letter and nowhere in Paul's letters to churches. It is needed more here. Timothy is about to be asked to come to Rome, to a man in chains whom most people have abandoned, and to take up a deposit that has cost its previous holder everything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To be “his prisoner” (v.8) rather than Rome's is Paul's settled way of describing custody (Eph 3:1; Philem 1). The chain is real and the ownership is not.

Now: Notice that a man facing execution begins his final letter with “the promise of the life.” That is not bravado; it is the letter's whole argument stated in its first sentence, and everything else — do not be ashamed, share in suffering, guard the deposit — rests on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a word of this letter is read, know where it comes from. Paul is in Rome, in prison, and this time he does not expect to come out. He will say so plainly in chapter 4: the time of his departure has come. These are the last written words we have from him.

And the first thing he says about himself is that he is an apostle “according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus.” A man facing execution opens his final letter by naming his commission in terms of life. That is not bravado; it is the whole argument of the letter stated in the first sentence.

“By the will of God” — the same ground as always. Whatever a Roman court decides about him, his appointment did not come from anywhere a court can reach.

Then the address, and it has softened since the first letter. There Timothy was “my true child in the faith” — genuine, as against the counterfeits then circulating in Ephesus. Here he is “my beloved child.” The polemical edge is gone. Paul is not establishing Timothy's standing against rivals now; he is writing to somebody he loves.

“Grace, mercy, and peace” — mercy again, as in the first letter and nowhere in the letters to churches. And it is needed more here than there. Timothy is about to be asked to come to Rome, to a man in chains whom most people have abandoned, and to take up a deposit that has cost its previous holder everything.

It is a very short greeting, and there is no thanksgiving for a church because there is no church in view. This is a personal letter from an old man to a younger one, written while there was still time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–14 — Fan Into Flame, and Guard the Deposit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul thanks the God his ancestors served, with a clear conscience, remembering Timothy constantly night and day (v.3) — and remembering his tears, longs to see him and be filled with joy (v.4). He recalls Timothy's sincere faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (v.5).

So he reminds him to fan into flame the gift given through the laying on of Paul's hands (v.6), since God gave a spirit not of timidity but of power and love and self-control (v.7). Therefore he is not to be ashamed of the testimony, nor of Paul his prisoner, but to share in suffering by God's power (v.8) — the God who saved and called us, not because of our works but by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before the ages began (v.9), now revealed through the appearing of our Saviour, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light (v.10).

For this Paul was appointed herald, apostle and teacher (v.11), and this is why he suffers — yet is not ashamed, for he knows whom he has believed and is convinced God can guard his deposit until that day (v.12). Timothy is to follow the pattern of sound words in faith and love (v.13), guarding the good deposit by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us (v.14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Deposits, Running Opposite Ways

Paratheke is the banking term from 1 Tim 6:20 — property left with a trustworthy man, to be returned exactly as received rather than developed or improved. It appears twice in this chapter, and the directions are opposite. In verse 12 Paul has entrusted something to God, and God is able to keep it. In verse 14 God has entrusted something to Timothy, and he must keep it — “by the Holy Spirit who dwells within us.” Both directions, same word, and the strength in both cases comes from the same place.

Verse 12's pronoun repays care: “I know whom I have believed”, not what. Paul's confidence at the end of his life does not rest on the soundness of his doctrine, though he fought for it in every letter he wrote. It rests on a person he is acquainted with. Doctrine matters enormously and it is not what a man leans on at the end; he leans on the one the doctrine is about.

And verses 9-10 are among the densest gospel statements in the New Testament. Grace was given “in Christ Jesus before the ages began” — not planned or intended but given, before there was a world in which we could exist to receive it, which removes any possibility that something we did since is the reason. Then it was “manifested” in history, and Christ “abolished death” — a verb meaning to render inoperative, in the past tense, written by a man on death row. Death still occurs; it no longer works.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 5 shows how the faith actually travelled. Acts tells us Timothy's mother was a believing Jewess and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1) — which almost certainly means the faith in that house came down the female line. Paul has spent two letters on overseers, deacons, ordination and public teaching; and the man he is entrusting everything to was formed by two women teaching a child at home, years before any of the machinery touched him. Nobody laid hands on Lois, and she is on no roll. He will make it explicit at 3:15: from childhood Timothy has known the sacred writings.

Now: The word in verse 7 is not the ordinary term for fear but deilia — cowardice, timidity, the shrinking that stops a man doing what he knows he should. Paul names it, which means it was there: Timothy was frightened, and the New Testament records it about one of its own leaders without embarrassment. The remedy is not “try to feel braver”. Paul tells a frightened man what he has been given — power because the task is beyond him, love because fear makes a man self-protective, and a sound mind because fear distorts judgement and a frightened man's estimate of his situation is almost never accurate. Note too that “fan into flame” implies embers, not ashes: the gift has not gone out, it needs air.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience.” Paul reaches back before his conversion. He does not treat his Jewish inheritance as a false start that Christ cancelled; the God he serves now is the God his forefathers served. The gospel was not a change of deity but the arrival of what that God had promised.

“With a clear conscience.” The letter to Ephesus made conscience a recurring test — the goal of the charge is love from a good conscience, and men who reject it make shipwreck (1 Tim 1:5, 19). Here Paul quietly claims the thing he required of others. It is the settled statement of a man at the end who has nothing outstanding.

“As I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day.” In a cell, with the hours empty, an old man prays for his friend at three in the morning. That is what the phrase means in practice.

Then verse 4, and it is one of the tenderest sentences Paul wrote: “As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.”

Somewhere there had been a parting, and Timothy had wept. Probably the last one, when Paul was taken. Paul remembers it, and the memory is precious rather than embarrassing to him. He does not tell Timothy that the tears were a weakness or that he should have borne it better.

“I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.” Not that Timothy may be comforted — that Paul may be. The man who has told other people to rejoice always, who is facing execution with composure, says openly that there is a joy he does not yet have and that a visit from this young man would supply it. Contentment in Paul never meant needing nobody.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I am reminded of your sincere faith” — anypokritos, un-play-acted, without a mask, the same word used of the faith the whole charge aims at in 1 Timothy 1:5. Whatever Timothy's timidity, Paul has no doubt his faith is the genuine article.

Then the two names, and this is one of the loveliest verses in the New Testament: “a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.”

Three generations, named. Acts tells us Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1) — which almost certainly means the father was not a believer, and that the faith in that house came down the female line. A grandmother, then a mother, then a boy who would carry the apostolic deposit into the next generation.

Weigh what that means about how the faith actually travels. Paul has spent two letters on overseers, deacons, elders, ordination and public teaching. And the man he is entrusting everything to was formed by two women teaching a child at home, years before any of the machinery touched him. Nobody laid hands on Lois. She is not on any roll. She taught her daughter, who taught her son, and the result is the letter you are reading.

Paul will make it explicit in chapter 3: from childhood Timothy has known the sacred writings (3:15). Somebody sat with him and taught him the Scriptures before he could read them himself, and it was not an apostle.

“And now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.” The verb dwells is the word for taking up residence — faith is not visiting Timothy, it lives there. And “I am sure” is Paul's own judgement, offered to a man who evidently needed to hear it. Some people require someone else to tell them that what they have is real.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God.” The verb means to rekindle, to stir a fire back into blaze — and it implies embers rather than ashes. Paul does not think the gift has gone out. He thinks it needs air.

That is a gentle diagnosis of a real condition. Timothy is not accused of unbelief or failure. He is a man whose fire has burned low — which happens to people who have been under pressure for a long time in a difficult post, and it is worth knowing that the apostolic response is not rebuke but stirring.

“Which is in you through the laying on of my hands.” Note the difference from the first letter, where the gift came “when the council of elders laid their hands on you” (1 Tim 4:14). Both are true — Paul was among them — but here he presses the personal connection, because that is what this letter is doing. The old man who commissioned him is about to die, and he wants Timothy to remember whose hands were on his head.

Then verse 7, which is the reason the fire had dimmed: “God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.”

The word is not the ordinary term for fear but deilia — cowardice, timidity, the shrinking that stops a man doing what he knows he should. Paul names it, which means it was there. Timothy was frightened, and the New Testament records it about one of its own leaders without embarrassment.

Against it, three gifts, and each answers something. Power — because the task is beyond him, and it always was. Love — because fear makes a man self-protective, and love is the only thing that reliably gets him outside himself. And self-control, sophronismos, a sound and disciplined mind — because fear distorts judgement, and a frightened man's estimate of his situation is almost never accurate.

The three together are the answer to timidity, and none of them is “try to feel braver”. Paul tells a frightened man what he has been given, not what he ought to summon.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore do not be ashamed.” The word governs this chapter — it comes three times (here, v.12, v.16) and shame is the pressure Timothy is under.

Two things he might be ashamed of, and they are named separately. First, “the testimony about our Lord” — the message itself, which in the Roman world meant announcing that a crucified provincial was Lord. Crucifixion was not a symbol then; it was the death reserved for slaves and rebels, and to preach it was to invite the response Paul got at Athens.

Second, and more pointedly: “nor of me his prisoner.” There is the real difficulty. Paul is in custody awaiting execution, and association with him is dangerous and humiliating. Verse 15 will say that everyone in Asia has already turned away. Timothy is being asked to be publicly connected to a condemned man at the exact moment when everyone else has decided not to be.

Note how Paul describes himself: not Rome's prisoner but his — the Lord's. The chain is real and the custody is Roman, but the ownership is not. He said the same thing from an earlier imprisonment (Eph 3:1; Philem 1).

“But share in suffering for the gospel.” The verb is a compound — suffer together with. Paul is not asking Timothy to be brave in his own separate trouble but to come and take a share of this one. It is an invitation into something, not merely an exhortation to endure.

And the clause that makes it possible: “by the power of God.” Not by Timothy's resolve. Paul has just said God gave a spirit of power (v.7), and here is where it is spent. The courage being asked for is not a quality Timothy must find in himself; it is a supply he is told to draw on.

verseByVerse.quote: who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has asked Timothy to suffer by the power of God — and then, characteristically, cannot mention God without describing him. What follows is one of the densest statements of the gospel in the New Testament, and it has the compression of something already sung.

“Who saved us and called us to a holy calling.” Both verbs are past and both are God's. Then the negative and the positive, and Paul is emphatic about the order: “not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace.”

“Which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began.” Stop there, because it is one of the most staggering phrases Paul ever wrote. Grace was given to us before time started. Not planned, not intended — given, in Christ Jesus, before there was any world in which we could exist to receive it. Whatever else that means, it removes the possibility that anything we have done since is the reason.

Then verse 10 brings it into history: “and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Saviour Christ Jesus.” The eternal purpose stayed hidden until a particular arrival. Epiphaneia is the shining-out word, used in that world of a god's or a king's public appearance.

“Who abolished death.” The verb means to render inoperative, to put out of action, to strip of power. And it is past tense — written by a man on death row. Paul does not say death has been made pleasant or that it will one day be dealt with. He says it has already been disarmed. It still occurs; it no longer works.

“And brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.” The image is of something switched on. Immortality was a hope people argued about — philosophers debated it, mystery cults sold it, tombstones denied it. Paul says it is no longer a matter of speculation, because it has been illuminated by an event.

And notice where this sits. Paul writes it to persuade a frightened young man to come and share his suffering. The argument is not “be brave”; it is “death has been abolished, so what exactly are they threatening you with?”

verseByVerse.quote: for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher, which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher” — herald, sent one, instructor, the same three offices as 1 Timothy 2:7. “Which is why I suffer as I do.” The suffering is not an interruption of the appointment; it is the consequence of it.

“But I am not ashamed.” There is the word again, and now Paul applies it to himself. He has told Timothy not to be ashamed of a prisoner; here he says the prisoner is not ashamed either. He is not asking the young man to bear something he is privately embarrassed about.

Then the sentence that has held Christians steady for two thousand years: “for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.”

Read the pronoun carefully. Not what I have believed — whom. Paul's confidence at the end of his life does not rest on the soundness of his doctrine, though he has fought for it in every letter. It rests on a person he is acquainted with. Doctrine matters enormously and it is not what you lean on at the end; you lean on the one the doctrine is about.

“He is able to guard.” The deposit language again (1 Tim 6:20), and here it runs the other way. Paul had a deposit to guard, and he tells Timothy in two verses to guard his. But underneath both is this: Paul has made a deposit with God, and God is keeping it. The guarding Christians do is real and it is not the guarding that finally counts.

What is the deposit he has left with God? He does not specify, and the ambiguity is probably deliberate — his own life, his converts, the gospel, all of it. Everything a man cannot hold on to himself, lodged with someone who can.

“Until that day.” Not until the trial, or until the executioner, or until things improve. Paul's horizon runs past his own death without pausing at it.

verseByVerse.quote: Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me.” The word is hypotyposis — an outline, a sketch, a model to work from, the same word Paul used of himself as the pattern of Christ's patience (1 Tim 1:16). Timothy is not being told to reproduce Paul's sentences verbatim; he is given a shape to keep to.

“Sound words” — the medical word again, healthy, wholesome. And “that you have heard from me”, which is the chain this letter keeps tracing: entrusted to Paul, heard by Timothy, to be handed on to faithful men who will teach others (2:2).

“In the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.” The pattern is not held in a vacuum. Doctrine kept without faith and love becomes exactly what the Ephesian teachers had — correct-sounding material producing envy and friction.

Then verse 14: “Guard the good deposit entrusted to you.” Paratheke, the banking term from 1 Timothy 6:20 — property left with a trustworthy man, to be returned exactly as received. Not developed, not improved. Returned.

And the clause that makes the command bearable: “by the Holy Spirit who dwells within us.” Timothy is not being asked to defend the faith with his own resources, which is just as well, since he is timid and Paul is about to die and everyone in Asia has left. The guarding is done by someone who lives inside the guard.

Set the two deposits side by side and the chapter's architecture appears. In verse 12 Paul has entrusted something to God, and God is able to keep it. In verse 14 God has entrusted something to Timothy, and he must keep it — by God's own Spirit. Both directions, same word, and the strength in both cases comes from the same place.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All who are in Asia have turned away from Paul, Phygelus and Hermogenes among them (v.15). But may the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains (v.16) — who on reaching Rome searched hard for him and found him (v.17); may the Lord grant him to find mercy on that day, and Timothy knows well all the service he rendered at Ephesus (v.18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Shame, and the Man Who Refused It

“Ashamed” governs this chapter, appearing three times — the pressure Timothy is under (v.8), the pressure Paul refuses (v.12), and here the pressure one man ignored (v.16). Note that Paul specifies the chains: it was the visible, humiliating, incriminating fact of the imprisonment that others could not stomach.

The turning away of verse 15 is probably not apostasy but personal desertion. Association with a man awaiting execution on a capital charge was genuinely dangerous, and people who had truly believed the gospel decided they could not afford to be connected with the prisoner — a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asia is the province whose capital is Ephesus, where Paul spent three years — longer than anywhere else — teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus until all the residents of the province had heard the word (Acts 19:10). His most fruitful work. And at the end they turned away. Phygelus and Hermogenes appear once in Scripture and it is here, for this; Paul evidently thought Timothy should know who they were, presumably because they were men he would otherwise have trusted.

Now: The detail that makes Onesiphorus unforgettable is in verse 17. Rome held perhaps a million people; a prisoner awaiting trial was listed nowhere convenient, and asking after a man on a capital charge meant drawing official attention to yourself. He went round the city making exactly the enquiries a sensible man would avoid, until he found him — and did it more than once. He preached no sermon we know of and held no office we are told about. Paul's prayer for a man who searched is that he would find mercy, and the echo is surely deliberate. That is this chapter's answer to shame, and it is available to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.”

It is one of the saddest verses in the New Testament, and it should not be hurried past. Asia is the province whose capital is Ephesus — where Paul spent three years, longer than anywhere else, teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus until all the residents of the province had heard the word (Acts 19:10). It was his most fruitful work.

And at the end, they turned away from him. “All” is doubtless a generalisation with exceptions — the next verse names one — but it is what it felt like from the cell.

The turning away is probably not apostasy. It reads as personal desertion: association with a man awaiting execution on a capital charge was dangerous, and people who had genuinely believed the gospel decided they could not afford to be connected with the prisoner. Which is a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.

Two names are given, and we know nothing else about them. Phygelus and Hermogenes appear once in Scripture, and it is here, for this. That is a sobering way to be remembered — and Paul evidently thought Timothy should know who they were, presumably because they were men Timothy would otherwise have trusted.

What matters most is the effect of this on the letter's central request. Paul is asking Timothy not to be ashamed of him (v.8) and to come to him (4:9, 21) — and he tells him plainly, before he asks, that everybody else has already declined. He does not conceal how isolated he is or make the invitation look more attractive than it is. He puts the cost on the table and then asks anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me— may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the desertion of verse 15, one man. “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus.”

We know nothing about him except these three verses and a passing mention in chapter 4. He is one of the minor figures of Scripture who exists in a sentence and turns out to be unforgettable.

Three things are said about him, and they build. “He often refreshed me” — the verb means to cool, to give respite, the relief of shade or water. Not once but often. Whatever the practical content — food, news, conversation, money — a man in a Roman cell was regularly made more comfortable because Onesiphorus kept turning up.

“And was not ashamed of my chains.” There is the chapter's word for the third time, and here it is answered. Everyone in Asia had been ashamed; this man was not. Note that Paul specifies the chains rather than the man — it was the visible, humiliating, incriminating fact of the imprisonment that others could not stomach.

“But when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me.” This is the detail that makes the portrait. Rome was a city of perhaps a million people; a prisoner awaiting trial was not listed anywhere convenient, and asking after a man on a capital charge meant drawing official attention to yourself. Onesiphorus went round Rome making exactly the enquiries a sensible man would avoid, until he found him.

“May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day.” Paul's prayer for a man who searched is that he would find — and the echo is surely deliberate. He sought Paul out; may he be sought out and shown mercy.

The chapter that began with a frightened young man and a deserted apostle ends with a portrait of one ordinary Christian who simply turned up. He preached no sermons we know of and held no office we are told about. He looked for a prisoner until he found him, and did it more than once, and was not embarrassed to be seen there. That is the answer this letter gives to shame, and it is available to anybody.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus,<sup>2</sup>To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day.<sup>4</sup>As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.<sup>5</sup>I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.<sup>6</sup>For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands,<sup>7</sup>for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.<sup>8</sup>Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,<sup>9</sup>who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began,<sup>10</sup>and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,<sup>11</sup>for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher,<sup>12</sup>which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.<sup>13</sup>Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.<sup>15</sup>You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.<sup>16</sup>May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains,<sup>17</sup>but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me—<sup>18</sup>may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.

2.title: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer: The Shape of Gospel Ministry
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Paul’s most concentrated instruction on the nature of gospel ministry. Three images in rapid succession — soldier, athlete, farmer — define the minister’s posture: single-mindedly devoted, rule-governed, and patiently laboring for a harvest that is certain though not yet visible. The minister is not someone who has found an easier life; they have exchanged one set of hardships for another and found the exchange worthwhile.

The chapter’s centre is the trustworthy saying of vv. 11–13 — almost certainly an early hymn known to Timothy — which holds together the certainty of future glory and the seriousness of present faithfulness. The logic of endurance is not stoic grit but eschatological confidence: if we died with him we will live with him; if we endure we will reign with him.

The second half of the chapter shifts to the pastoral work of handling false teachers and navigating community conflict. The worker approved by God rightly handles the word of truth, avoids quarrelling, and corrects opponents with gentleness, recognising that God may yet grant them repentance. The minister’s posture toward error is not the prosecutor’s fury but the physician’s patience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” — the chapter opens with the resource before the command. Timothy is not told to find strength in himself but in grace — the unearned, freely-given enabling power of God flowing from union with Christ. The first obligation is transmission: what Timothy has heard from Paul is to be entrusted to faithful men who will teach others also. The four-generation chain (Paul → Timothy → faithful men → others) is the shape of the Great Commission in miniature: the gospel travels person to person; the deposit is passed hand to hand.

Three metaphors of ministry: the soldier who does not entangle himself in civilian affairs; the athlete who competes according to the rules; the farmer who is first to receive a share of the crops. Each emphasises a different facet: the soldier speaks of single-minded dedication (no divided loyalties); the athlete of rule-governed competition (winning the wrong way disqualifies); the farmer of patient, laboring confidence (the harvest comes to those who plant and wait). Together they describe the minister: devoted, disciplined, and patient toward a future that is certain but not yet visible.

The trustworthy saying of vv. 11–13 is a four-line poem, probably an early baptismal or martyr hymn already known to Timothy. Its structure is conditional — if/then — moving from the most confident (if we died with him) to the most sobering (if we deny him) to the most mysterious (if we are faithless, he remains faithful). This last line does not nullify the third; it speaks of the unchangeableness of Christ’s own character: he is faithful to his word, which means both that his warnings are real and that his grace toward those who truly belong to him is real.
verseByVerse.theology: Transmission as Faithfulness. The four-generation chain of v. 2 is not merely a practical strategy for church growth; it is a theology of deposit. The gospel is not an experience to be had but a trust to be transmitted, and transmission requires both reception (Paul to Timothy) and selection — the transmission is entrusted to “faithful men who will be able to teach others,” not merely to enthusiastic ones. Faithfulness is the primary qualification because the content must be preserved, not merely the energy. The minister who values passion over precision in transmission has misunderstood what is being transmitted.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Timothy was in Ephesus, a city of commerce, religion, and philosophy. The temptations to entanglement in civilian concerns — to find significance in social standing, to trim the gospel for the philosophical marketplace, to measure success by Ephesian standards — were constant. Paul’s three metaphors address exactly these temptations. Now: The minister tempted to build a ministry around personality, cultural trend, or social acceptability rather than patient, faithful, rule-governed gospel transmission is the soldier who has gone into business, the athlete who has decided the rules do not apply, the farmer who is in a hurry. The chapter is not anti-relevance; it is anti-substitution.

verseByVerse.quote: You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Be strengthened” (endynamou) — present imperative, passive voice: be continually empowered, keep receiving strength. The posture is receptive, not self-generating; strength is not manufactured but received from the grace that is in Christ Jesus. “In the presence of many witnesses” — Paul emphasises the public, verifiable, non-private character of what he has transmitted; the gospel is not an esoteric teaching for the initiated. “Faithful men who will be able to teach others” — two qualifications: faithfulness (character, reliability to the deposit) and ability to teach (competence in transmission). Both are necessary; neither is sufficient alone. The four generations (Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others) are the structural shape of all genuine apostolic succession: not institutional transfer of office but personal transmission of truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him. An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three metaphors, three principles. The soldier’s principle: not entanglement in civilian affairs (pragmateiais tou biou — the affairs of ordinary life). This does not prohibit ministers from having families or responsibilities; it forbids the divided loyalty that puts ministry in second place when the costs of first place become real. The aim is to please the one who enlisted (stratologēsanti — the one who recruited, enrolled) — Christ, not the congregation. The athlete’s principle: competes according to the rules (nomimōs) — not merely wins but competes correctly; the method matters, not just the result. Paul has in mind those who cut theological corners, compromise content for popularity, or win arguments at the cost of truth. The farmer’s principle: hard work first, harvest second. The farmer who plants does not eat until harvest, but the farmer who plants does eat — the harvest is certain; the priority of labour is simply the order in which certainty is realised. “The Lord will give you understanding” — the practical wisdom to apply these metaphors is itself a gift; Timothy is asked to think hard, and promised that God will illuminate what he ponders.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound! Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David” — a compressed creed, two phrases balanced: risen from the dead (his victory over death) and offspring of David (his humanity, his Messianic covenant lineage). Paul tells Timothy to remember, as if the resurrection of Christ is precisely the thing most easily forgotten under pressure. “Bound with chains as a criminal” — the word kakourgos (criminal, wrongdoer) is the same word used of the two men crucified beside Jesus (Luke 23:33). Paul is a kakourgos in Nero’s eyes. But: “the word of God is not bound.” The chain on the apostle cannot chain the message; the gospel moves even when its herald is immobilised. “I endure everything for the sake of the elect” — the doctrine of election is here the motivation for missionary and pastoral endurance: there are people yet to be gathered; their gathering is certain; Paul’s suffering is the cost of the harvest that will come. Election is not the end of mission but its engine.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself.
verseByVerse.commentary: The “trustworthy saying” formula (pistos ho logos — reliable is the word) marks this as a received, fixed formulation — one of five in the Pastoral Epistles (1 Tim 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; Titus 3:8). The four-line structure moves from assurance to sobriety to mystery. Line one: “if we died with him” — baptismal language (Rom 6:3–8); the union in death that guarantees union in resurrection. Line two: “if we endure, we will also reign” — the condition is real endurance; the promise is not merely life but shared dominion with the enthroned Christ. Line three: “if we deny him, he also will deny us” — the echo of Matthew 10:33 (Jesus’s own logion); this is not mild. Line four: “if we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself” — the most debated line. It does not nullify line three; it speaks of Christ’s own unchanging character, which guarantees both that his warnings are real (he is faithful to his word) and that his grace toward those who truly belong to him cannot be abandoned (he is faithful to the covenant sealed with his own blood). The mystery is not resolved but held: perseverance matters, and Christ’s faithfulness undergirds those who persevere.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — A Worker Approved by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second half of the chapter applies the theological grounding of vv. 1–13 to the specific pastoral challenge of false teaching and community conflict. Paul’s first instruction is negative: stop quarrelling about words (logomachein) — it does no good and ruins the hearers. The contrast is the worker who “rightly handles” (orthotomountas) the word of truth — literally “cuts straight,” a hapax legomenon whose exact background is disputed (road-building? tent-making? ploughing a straight furrow?) but whose meaning is clear: the word is to be handled with skill and precision so that the truth reaches where it is needed without distortion.

The false teaching of Hymenaeus and Philetus is described precisely: they claim the resurrection has already happened. This is a proto-gnostic realised eschatology that spiritualises the future bodily resurrection away, collapsing the whole eschatological structure of the gospel. Paul calls it gangrene (gangraina) — the tissue death that spreads and destroys surrounding healthy flesh. Against it stands the firm foundation of God (v. 19) with its double inscription: the Lord knows those who are his (divine sovereignty over his own, echoing Num 16:5), and everyone who names the Lord’s name must depart from iniquity (human moral obligation of those who belong).

The practical counsel for navigating this situation is dense: flee youthful passions; pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace; have nothing to do with foolish controversies; be patient; correct opponents with gentleness. The governing image of the vessel (vv. 20–21) gives the theological basis: the minister who cleanses himself from dishonourable patterns becomes a vessel set apart as holy, useful to the master, ready for every good work.
verseByVerse.theology: Orthotomia: The Skill of Straight Cutting. The hapax orthotomountas (rightly handling, cutting straight) in v. 15 names what distinguishes the approved worker from the quarreller about words. False teachers also use Scripture, but carelessly, twisting it to support their innovations. The minister who cuts straight knows the difference between an accurate representation of the text and an impressive-sounding use of the text. This is both a practical skill — acquired through patient, disciplined study — and a theological duty, because the word is not the minister’s possession to deploy as he sees fit; it is God’s trust, to be presented with the care due to the one who gave it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hymenaeus and Philetus were real people in Timothy’s community, and their “already resurrection” error was not abstract; people Timothy knew were being unsettled by it. Paul’s instruction is not primarily to win the argument but to help the unsettled stand on the firm foundation of God’s sovereignty and the community’s moral clarity. Now: The minister navigating theological novelty in their congregation needs both the firm foundation Paul describes and the gentle correction he prescribes. The goal is never to humiliate the one in error but to see them “recover their senses” (anannēpsōsin — sober up from drunkenness) and escape the snare of the devil. The false teacher is not an enemy to be destroyed but a prisoner to be freed.

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers. Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Quarrel about words” (logomachein) — a compound found only here and in 1 Tim 6:4; it names theological debate more interested in winning than in truth. The diagnostic is outcome: it “does no good and ruins the hearers” (epi katastrophē tōn akouontōn — to the overturning, the catastrophe, of those who hear). “Do your best” (spoudason — make haste, be diligent) — the approved worker is not passive; he works hard at the craft. “Rightly handling” (orthotomountas) — the Greek literally means cutting straight; used in Proverbs 3:6 and 11:5 (LXX) for making straight paths. The word-handler’s skill is to direct the truth to where it is needed without deflection or distortion. “Irrelevant babble” (bebelōus kenophonĪas — profane empty sounds) — teaching that sounds significant but carries no weight of truth; it does not stay at the level of neutrality but actively leads people further into ungodliness.

verseByVerse.quote: and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some. But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Hymenaeus (mentioned also in 1 Tim 1:20 as delivered to Satan for discipline) and Philetus are named because Timothy needs to know specifically who is teaching error. Their error: “the resurrection has already happened” (anastasin ēdē gegonenai) — a realised eschatology that spiritualises the future bodily resurrection into a present spiritual experience. This collapses the whole forward-oriented structure of the gospel — the body matters, the future matters, the return of Christ matters. Paul calls it gangraina (gangrene) — tissue death that spreads and destroys healthy flesh around it; false teaching is not merely incorrect but actively destructive. Against it stands the firm foundation of God (v. 19) with a double inscription: first, the Lord’s sovereignty over his own (egnō kyrios tous ontas autou — from Num 16:5, spoken in the context of Korah’s rebellion, confirming that God knows who truly belongs to him regardless of community confusion); second, the community’s moral obligation (aphostētō apo adikias — depart from iniquity). Divine sovereignty and human responsibility inscribed on the same foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work. So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
verseByVerse.commentary: The household metaphor is practical: a great house contains every kind of vessel, honourable and dishonorable. The distinction is not about predestination but about present fitness for use. The minister who cleanses himself from the patterns of false teaching (ean tis ekkatharē heauton apo toutōn) — by separation from the quarrelling, the gangrene, the empty babble — makes himself a vessel set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work. Fitness for service depends on purity; purity is the minister’s responsibility. “Flee youthful passions” — these are not primarily sexual; the passions of the immature include the desire for influence, the hunger for theological novelty, the need to win arguments, the craving for recognition. “Pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace — along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart”: the pursuit of virtue is located in community, not in isolated self-improvement. You cannot pursue these things alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Foolish and ignorant controversies” — mōras (foolish, moronic) because they produce nothing of value; apaideutos (uneducated, undisciplined) because they reflect an untrained engagement with truth. “The Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome” (amachon — literally not-fighting) — Paul is prescribing not politeness but a fundamentally non-combative orientation: the minister’s goal is not to defeat the opponent but to see the opponent freed. “Correcting his opponents with gentleness” (en prautēti paideuonta) — gentle correction is not soft correction; it is correction aimed at the other person’s good rather than the minister’s triumph. The outcome is God’s responsibility: “God may perhaps grant them repentance” — the humility of “perhaps” places the result where it belongs. “Come to their senses” (anannēpsōsin — to sober up from drunkenness) — the false teacher is not an enemy to be destroyed but a prisoner, captured by the devil, who may yet be rescued from the snare.

3.title: Perilous Times and the God-Breathed Word
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens with one of Paul’s most disturbing prophetic passages and closes with one of his most enduring theological affirmations. The juxtaposition is deliberate: the darkness of the description of last-days humanity (vv. 1–9) makes the light of God-breathed Scripture (vv. 16–17) shine all the more brilliantly.

The eighteen vices of vv. 2–5 are a systematic anatomy of godlessness — not paganism but religious godlessness, people who maintain a form of godliness while denying its power. This is the most dangerous kind of false Christianity: externally plausible, internally hollow, and capable of leading astray those who are “always learning but never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.”

The corrective Paul offers is not a better technique but a deeper anchor: Paul’s own pattern of faith and suffering (vv. 10–12), the solid ground of Scripture received from childhood (vv. 14–15), and the character of Scripture itself as the God-breathed word adequate for everything the minister needs (vv. 16–17). The last-days situation calls not for innovation but for deeper rootedness in what has been given.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Godlessness in the Last Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“In the last days difficult times will come” — Paul is not predicting a distant future era but describing the character of the entire age between Christ’s first and second comings, intensifying toward the end. The eighteen characteristics of godlessness that follow are not a description of secular society but of people who are “having a form of godliness” — they are inside or at the margins of the church, using the language and structures of Christian community for purposes the gospel was never meant to serve.

The list is structured by disordered love: it begins with “lovers of self” and ends with “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God.” The frame brackets every vice in the catalog: at the root of each is a love directed at the wrong object. Augustine’s theology of disordered loves is embedded here: the problem is not that people love themselves or pleasure, but that these loves have displaced the love of God as the governing orientation of life.

Jannes and Jambres (v. 8) are not named in the canonical Old Testament. The names come from Jewish tradition — the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 7:11, fragments at Qumran, and Pliny — identifying them as the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses. Paul’s allusion assumes this tradition is known and recognises in the false teachers the same pattern: counterfeit power opposing genuine revelation. The judgment on Jannes and Jambres was exposure — “their folly was made plain to all” — and the same fate awaits the false teachers of Timothy’s community.
verseByVerse.theology: Form Without Power: The Most Dangerous Religion. The “form of godliness without power” (morphōsin eusebeias… tēn de dynamin autēs ērnēmenoi) is Paul’s sharpest diagnostic of religious self-deception. The power of genuine godliness is the transforming power of the gospel — the cross and resurrection actually doing their work in human lives, producing genuine repentance, genuine love, genuine self-denial. Where these are absent and the form remains, the shell is there but the life has gone. This is a diagnostic for churches, not only for obvious heretics.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The false teachers in Ephesus had genuine religiosity — they used Christian language, attended gatherings, perhaps had impressive spiritual credentials. The community had difficulty distinguishing them from genuine believers, which is why Paul’s list is so detailed: the distinction is not in external religion but in the internal orientation of love and the presence of genuine transformation. Now: Every generation produces its form-without-power Christianity: theologically sophisticated, institutionally stable, socially acceptable, and morally unremarkable. The tests remain Paul’s: not “does this person know the right words?” but “is there genuine love of God rather than love of self? Is there genuine transformation rather than religious performance?”

verseByVerse.quote: But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty. For people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power. Avoid such people.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Difficult” (chalepoi) — the same word used of the Gadarene demoniac (Matt 8:28 — “fierce”); these are not merely uncomfortable times but dangerous ones, pressing against human welfare and spiritual health. The catalog of eighteen vices cascades without pause but is framed by disordered love: the list opens with “lovers of self” (philautoi) and closes with “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God” (philhēdonoi mâllon ē philotheoi). Everything in between — pride, slander, brutality, treachery — is the outworking of this inversion: when self replaces God as the supreme love, every other love and obligation is eventually distorted. The climax — “having a form of godliness but denying its power” — is the most disturbing because it places these people inside religious communities. “Avoid such people” (apotrēpou — turn away from, avoid) is the practical counsel: not engagement as if persuasion were still possible with those fully hardened to the form, but separation.

verseByVerse.quote: For among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women, burdened with sins and led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth. Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith. But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Creep into households” (endynousin eis tas oikias) — the verb suggests stealthy infiltration rather than open entry. “Weak women” (gynaikaria) — the diminutive is dismissive of the false teachers’ targeting strategy, not of women themselves; Paul is exposing the predatory pattern of manipulation. Those targeted are “burdened with sins and led astray by various passions” and “always learning but never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth” — the pattern of spiritual manipulation: cultivate dependence, offer the appearance of progress, prevent genuine arrival at the truth. Jannes and Jambres: their names appear not in the canonical Old Testament but in Jewish tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, Exod 7:11; also at Qumran and in Pliny the Elder). They are the magicians of Pharaoh’s court who replicated Moses’ signs by counterfeit power. The parallel is exact: false teachers oppose genuine revelation with impressive-seeming alternatives. But the judgment is equally certain: “their folly will be plain to all.” Exposure is itself a mercy to the community confused by them.

"Always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth" — the Greek draws a precise distinction. Pantote manthanonta (always in the process of learning, continuously accumulating teaching) is set against eis epignōsin alētheias elthein dynamenon (able to come into epignōsis of truth). Epignōsis is not just gnōsis (knowledge, information) but full, deep, relational recognition — the kind of knowing that transforms, the knowing of 2 Pet 1:2–3 that produces "all things pertaining to life and godliness." The women Paul describes are caught in perpetual intake without this arrival: they receive teaching but are never changed by it, never arrive at the confrontation with truth that would expose their sins, discipline their passions, and set them free. False teachers are experts at facilitating this condition: they offer a constant stream of spiritual-sounding content that feels like learning but never reaches the nerve of conviction and repentance. The diagnostic for a congregation is not how much teaching they receive but whether they are being changed by it — whether epignōsis is happening, or only manthanein.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Scripture and the Man of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Against the false teachers’ pattern Paul sets his own pattern — not as self-promotion but as the concrete human embodiment of the life he is calling Timothy to. “You have followed” (parēkolouthēsas — you have observed closely, traced, followed alongside) my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness. Timothy has seen these things; and what he has seen includes persecutions and sufferings, not their absence. The pattern of apostolic existence is not immunity from suffering but deliverance through it.

The connection between Paul’s suffering and the normative Christian life is explicit: “all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (v. 12). This is not a possibility but a normative expectation for every generation. Evil people will go from bad to worse. The answer is not pessimism but rootedness: “but as for you, continue in what you have learned.” The contrast between the downward trajectory of apostasy and the upward anchoring of the man of God is the chapter’s structural spine.

The theological culmination is vv. 16–17, where Paul grounds the minister’s adequacy in the character of Scripture. Theopneustos — God-breathed — is almost certainly Paul’s own coinage: the word appears nowhere in Greek literature before this letter. The metaphor is expiration, not inspiration in the usual sense: Scripture came out of God’s mouth, breathed out from the source of all truth. And it is profitable for four specific purposes that together cover everything the minister needs: teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness.
verseByVerse.theology: Theopneustos: The Exhalation of God. The doctrine of Scripture as the breath of God is the Pauline foundation of the Reformation’s sola scriptura. It does not claim the human authors were passive — 2 Peter 1:21 insists on both human agency and divine movement. It claims that the result — the text we have — carries the full authority of God himself, because he breathed it out. The fourfold use maps onto negative and positive, doctrinal and practical: teaching (positive doctrinal formation), reproof (negative exposure of error and sin), correction (epanorthōsin — re-straightening, restoring to the right position), and training in righteousness (paideia — the whole formative process of bringing a person to maturity). Together they constitute the complete equipment of the minister.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Timothy had learned Scripture from childhood through Lois and Eunice — not as an academic exercise but as the medium through which he had come to faith in “Christ Jesus.” The “sacred writings” he knew were the Old Testament, and Paul’s argument is that these same writings, read through their Christological fulfilment, contain “the wisdom for salvation.” The continuity of Old and New Testament Scripture is implicit in the argument. Now: The minister who spends little time in Scripture and much time in cultural analysis, leadership books, and self-improvement literature has inverted the supply chain. The “equipped for every good work” (exērtismenos — thoroughly fitted out, completely outfitted) is Paul’s promise to the minister who makes Scripture central. Nothing else equips like this.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra — which persecutions I endured; yet from them all the Lord rescued me. Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.
verseByVerse.commentary: “You have followed” (parēkolouthēsas) — not merely “you know about” but you have traced, observed closely, followed alongside; Timothy’s knowledge of Paul is personal and particular. The persecutions at Antioch (Acts 13:50), Iconium (Acts 14:5), and Lystra (Acts 14:19 — where Paul was stoned, dragged outside the city, and left for dead) are events Timothy witnessed or heard about firsthand, since Lystra was his home city. The rescue is not from suffering but through suffering; Paul was stoned and left for dead, and he survived. The rescue is the resurrection pattern applied to apostolic existence: through death to life. “All who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (v. 12) — the future passive is almost a definition: carrying the gospel’s offense into a world that rejects it means the world will push back. This is normative, not exceptional.

verseByVerse.quote: while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Evil people and impostors will go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived” — the trajectory of apostasy is self-reinforcing: the lie told to others is first told to oneself; the deceiver is also deceived, and the deception deepens. “But as for you” (sy de — the emphatic personal contrast, appearing in 2:1 and 4:5 as well) — Timothy is to continue (mene — remain, abide, stay) in what he has learned. The ground of this continuing is twofold: from whom he learned it (Paul, Lois, Eunice — trusted witnesses) and what it has done (the sacred writings have made him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus). “Wise for salvation” (sophisai eis sōtērian) — the wisdom Scripture gives is not general human wisdom but the specific knowledge that leads to salvation; and that salvation comes through faith in Christ Jesus, not through the writings themselves. The Scriptures are the instrument; Christ is the object.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary: “All Scripture is breathed out by God” (pasa graphē theopneustos) — the adjective theopneustos is a Pauline coinage, appearing nowhere in Greek literature before this letter. The metaphor is expiration: Scripture came out of the mouth of God, breathed out from the source of all truth, rather than having divine breath put into it from outside. This does not exclude the human authors (2 Pet 1:21 insists on both human agency and the Spirit’s movement) but claims that the result — the text — carries the full authority of God himself. The fourfold use covers both doctrinal and practical, negative and positive: teaching (positive instruction in truth), reproof (elenchos — confronting error and sin), correction (epanorthōsis — literally re-straightening, restoring to right position), training in righteousness (paideia — the whole formative process of raising a person to full moral maturity, as a parent forms a child). “The man of God” (ho tou theou anthrōpos) — a technical Old Testament term for the prophet, applied here to the minister who handles Scripture. “Complete, equipped for every good work” (artios… exērtismenos) — artios means perfectly fitted, lacking nothing; exartizō means to furnish completely, outfit fully. The minister shaped by Scripture lacks nothing necessary for the work.

4.title: Preach the Word: The Commission, the Crown, and the Cloak
4.overview:
The final chapter of 2 Timothy is Paul’s most personal and most urgent. He has told Timothy what the gospel is, what the minister must do, what Scripture provides, and what opposition to expect. Now he gives the direct commission — preach the word — and then, with the unsentimental clarity of a man who can see the end of the road, he describes where that commission has brought him: not to triumph but to the threshold of death, with a faithful conscience and an unflinching confidence in the one who has been his judge all along.

The charge of vv. 1–8 is the most solemn in the Pauline corpus. The invocation of God and Christ Jesus as witnesses, the eschatological framework of the appearing and the kingdom, the urgency of “in season and out of season” — these are not administrative instructions; they are the last words of a man who has paid every cost the commission demanded and now calls his successor to pay the same.

The final section (vv. 9–22) is the most humanly moving passage Paul ever wrote. The request for the cloak and the books. The notice of Demas’s defection — devastating in its compression. “Only Luke is with me.” The greetings sent and received. The final benediction: “The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.” Paul has written great theology; but he ends with a cloak, a few friends, and the grace of Christ. It is enough.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul charges Timothy “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom.” Four witnesses are invoked: God himself, Christ Jesus the coming Judge, his appearing (the Parousia as present reality pressing into the commission), and his kingdom. No human minister has ever been given a commission in more solemn terms. The weight of the charge is deliberate: “preach the word” is backed by the authority of the universe’s coming Judge.

The command is comprehensive in its timing (in season and out of season) and in its modes: reprove, rebuke, exhort — three distinct tools for three distinct needs. The urgency is eschatological: the time is already coming when people will not endure sound teaching but accumulate teachers to suit their passions. “Itching ears” (kēthomenoĪ tēn akoēn — having their hearing scratched) is a medical metaphor for the pleasure of being told what one wants to hear. The minister who capitulates to itching ears has denied the congregation the one medicine that can actually heal.

Paul’s own testimony in vv. 6–8 is the most dignified farewell in the New Testament. Three perfect tenses: I have fought, I have finished, I have kept. These are completed actions with ongoing effects: the fight is over; the finish stands; the keeping is accomplished. And waiting: the crown of righteousness, which the Lord the righteous Judge will award on that Day — not only to Paul but to all who have loved his appearing.
verseByVerse.theology: The Parousia as the Frame of the Preaching Commission. The appearing of Christ is the theological frame of vv. 1–8. The minister preaches not to an audience of human beings but before the face of the coming Christ who will judge the living and the dead. This is both the ultimate accountability (nothing is hidden from him) and the ultimate freedom (the minister’s obligation is to the Judge, not to the audience’s approval). The Reformed tradition has consistently held that faithfulness in ministry is defined not by results but by fidelity to the commission — and the commission will be assessed not at the next elders’ meeting but at the appearing of the Lord.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul could see the direction the church was moving — toward teachers who would tell people what they wanted to hear — and Timothy needed to be steeled against the path of audience-pleasing ministry. The charge “preach the word” is the alternative to what the false teachers were offering: not novelty, not entertainment, not therapeutic reassurance, but the word of God in all its breadth and depth. Now: The itching-ears passage is not a description of the world outside the church; it describes what happens inside the church when the word is evacuated. The crown of righteousness is awarded to those who loved his appearing — which means being more concerned with his assessment than with the congregation’s approval.

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary: “I charge you” (diamartyromai) — the verb carries legal and covenantal weight: I solemnly testify, I earnestly charge with full witness. “In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus” — God the Father and the Son are the witnesses; the commission is made before the ultimate tribunal. “Who is to judge the living and the dead” (ton mellonta krinein zōntas kai nekrous) — the future active participle: the one who is about to judge; the judgment presses into the present from the future. “Preach the word” (kēruxon ton logon) — the aorist imperative, sharp and direct. “In season and out of season” (eukairōs akairōs) — a rhetorical pairing of opposites meaning always, regardless of convenience or inconvenience. Elengxon (reprove — confront and expose what is wrong), epitimēson (rebuke — admonish with authority), parakaleson (exhort — come alongside and urge forward): three distinct modes for three distinct pastoral needs. Complete patience (en pasē makrothymia) and teaching are the manner and the content; the preaching that reproves and rebukes without patience destroys; the patience without content is empty.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths. As for you, always be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Sound teaching” (hygiainousēs didaskalĪs) — the medical metaphor: doctrine that promotes spiritual health, doctrine that heals rather than flatters. The accumulation of teachers “to suit their own passions” (kata tas idĪas epithymias) is not random; it is driven by desire. People who want comfort find teachers who provide it; people who want permission find teachers who grant it. “Itching ears” (kēthomenoi tēn akoēn) — the itch is in the hearing itself, a craving to be tickled rather than taught. “Wander off into myths” (eis tous mythous ektrapēsontai) — the passive suggests not deliberate apostasy but the drift that results from following desires rather than truth: no one intends to end up in myth; they simply keep choosing what feels good. “As for you” (sy de — the emphatic personal contrast for the third time in the letter): be sober-minded (nēphe — stay alert, don’t be intoxicated by the surrounding culture), endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfil your ministry. The four imperatives are the counter-description to the itching-ears world: this is what the faithful minister does while everyone else chases what they want.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that Day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Poured out as a drink offering” (spendōmai — present passive, continuous action) — the libation was poured beside the burnt offering in the Jewish sacrificial system (Num 15:5; 28:7); Paul used the same metaphor in Philippians 2:17 when martyrdom was only possible. Now it is certain: the pouring is nearly complete. “The time of my departure” (ho kairos tēs analúses mou) — analúsis means an untying, a loosening: the releasing of a ship from its moorings, the striking of a tent, the freeing of an animal from its yoke. Death is not an ending but a departure, a setting out for home. The three perfect tenses are Paul’s epitaph written by himself: I have fought (tōn kalōn agōna ēgōnisamai — the noun and verb from the same root: the good contest I have contested), I have finished, I have kept. “The crown of righteousness” — the genitive is best read as the righteous crown, the crown that is the Lord’s right and righteous gift: not earned by moral superiority but awarded by the Righteous Judge to those who have loved his appearing. And — crucially — not only to Paul: “not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.” The crown is not a prize for exceptional apostolic achievement; it is the gift of every faithful Christian life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — Final Instructions: Loss, Faithfulness, and Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section of the letter is the most humanly immediate. Paul asks Timothy to come quickly, to bring Mark, to pick up the cloak left at Troas, and to bring the books — especially the parchments. These are the requests of a real man who is cold, lonely, and not yet finished reading. The detail of the cloak at Troas has moved readers across the centuries: not a theological symbol but a practical need, the bodily coldness of a prisoner awaiting execution.

The human landscape of the section is defined by loss and faithfulness. Loss: Demas has deserted, “in love with this present world” — agapēsas ton nyn aiōna, the aorist of decisive, completed abandonment. Crescens and Titus are gone. Alexander has done great harm. At Paul’s first defence, no one stood with him. But: Luke alone is faithful. Mark — the same Mark whose inadequacy caused the rupture between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39) — is now “very useful” for ministry. The rehabilitation is complete. Grace can restore.

The great promise of v. 18 — “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom” — is not a promise of escape from execution but of preservation through it: Paul will not be lost on his way to the kingdom. And the final benediction — “The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you” — is the simplest and most complete ending Paul could have written. Spirit and grace: the two things the minister most needs and cannot manufacture.
verseByVerse.theology: “Only Luke Is with Me”: The Theology of Apostolic Loneliness.
