The four words of v. 11 are among the most pastorally significant Paul ever wrote, because they tell us that even the greatest of apostolic servants experienced the deepest human loneliness. Paul did not have a large, loyal team at the end; he had one faithful friend. The theology embedded in this is the theology of the whole letter: the gospel does not guarantee earthly comfort, human loyalty, or institutional support. It guarantees the presence of the one who stands by us when all others desert: “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (v. 17). The Lord’s presence is not contingent on the presence of friends.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The people Paul names in vv. 9–22 are the real infrastructure of the early church: Priscilla and Aquila, who had risked their necks for Paul (Rom 16:4); Erastus, possibly the city treasurer of Corinth (Rom 16:23); Trophimus, an Ephesian left sick at Miletus. These are not types but persons; the ministry Paul exercised was a network, not a solo operation. The loss of parts of that network (Demas, the Asian churches) made the remaining parts all the more precious. Now: The minister who builds their ministry as a solo operation has not learned from Paul’s network; but the minister who is shattered when their network fails has not learned from Paul’s theology of the Lord who stands by when all others have gone. Both the network and the Lord’s sufficiency are real; neither replaces the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to come to me soon. For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry… When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments. Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me” — agapēsas (having loved) is the aorist of decisive, completed action; this is not wandering but departure. Ton nyn aiōna — the present age, the world-system as it now stands — is what has captured Demas’s love. The contrast with v. 8 is quiet but devastating: the one who loves Christ’s appearing endures to the end; the one who loves the present age cannot. The same co-worker mentioned with warmth in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24 ends here in three words of sorrow. “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry” — the rehabilitation is complete. This is the John Mark who had turned back from the first mission (Acts 13:13), whose inadequacy caused Paul and Barnabas to separate (Acts 15:37–39). Decades later, Paul calls him “very useful” (eychrestos — good-for-something, serviceable). The cloak (phailonēn — a heavy outer garment, probably of thick wool) and the books (bibliois) and especially the parchments (membranas — possibly Old Testament scrolls or Paul’s own notes) are the requests of a man who is cold and who intends to keep reading and writing until the end. “The Lord will repay him according to his deeds” — not a curse but a release of the matter to the only tribunal that finally counts.

verseByVerse.quote: At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them! But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion’s mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: “At my first defense no one came to stand by me” — the prōtē apologia may be the preliminary hearing before the full trial; Paul stands alone. The echo of Gethsemane is audible: the disciples sleeping, the friends fleeing, Jesus alone. Paul makes the same prayer the cross teaches: “May it not be charged against them” — not bitterness but the prayer of forgiveness. “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (parestē moi ho kyrios kai enedynamosen me) — when all human support was removed, divine support remained. The Lord’s presence is the answer to every form of abandonment. “Rescued from the lion’s mouth” — whether a metaphor for Nero’s power or a reference to a literal arena encounter, the rescue was real and the pattern is the same: through the mouth of danger, not around it. “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom” — not rescue from execution (Paul expects to die) but rescue through it; the kingdom-arrival is the destination, and no evil deed can prevent it. The doxology that follows (to him be the glory) is Paul’s last burst of praise: the God who has stood by him through everything deserves the glory of everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus stayed at Corinth, and I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus. Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final greetings are the map of a ministry spread across the Mediterranean world: Prisca and Aquila (who had risked their lives for Paul, Rom 16:4; now apparently back in Ephesus after years in Corinth and Rome), the household of Onesiphorus (his courageous friend of 1:16–18), Erastus (possibly the city treasurer of Corinth, Rom 16:23), Trophimus from Ephesus (Acts 20:4) left sick at Miletus — a reminder that even apostolic companions suffer illness; Paul did not always heal. “Come before winter” (pro cheimōnos) — the closing of the shipping lanes would make travel impossible; Paul wants Timothy before then. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia: names otherwise unknown to us, members of the Roman church who add their greetings. Linus is identified by Irenaeus and Tertullian as the first bishop of Rome after Peter — a tantalising detail. The final benediction — “The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you” — is Paul’s last written words. Spirit and grace: the two things the minister most needs and cannot manufacture. The Lord provides both. The letter that opened with dying instructions ends with the assurance that the one who gave the commission will also give the strength to keep it.
